name: Emeka Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine by me. I've filled in union surveys before, but nobody's ever asked me what I think off the record. Go on, then.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm herdsman at Brookfield, a mixed farm owned by a farmers' co-op, about 450 hectares with 180 dairy cows, wheat, barley and some oilseed. I'm in the parlour by half four, milking with Piotr, then feeding, checking the calving pens and scraping out. In spring and harvest I'm on the tractor half the day too. The cows I love; the paperwork wears me out, and I still keep the calving diary on paper because I don't trust the app.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ama on Mill Lane, and she's a nurse at the county hospital, so between us we're on decent money. I've got over a year of wages put by, plus a share of my grandad's twelve acres that we rent to a neighbour. I'm the union rep for the farm staff, which mostly means arguing about overtime and boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That's what I've been telling Piotr for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the canteen: told you so. The tech firms promised the moon and gave us a smarter spreadsheet. A computer that can't calve a heifer at three in the morning was never going to take my job. I'd probably put something like that on the union group chat too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life carries on, and that suits me. The co-op pays well, there are farms all round us crying out for good stockmen, and Ama's job isn't going anywhere. The one thing I'd watch is whether the manager uses any saved time as an excuse to cut a body from the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep milking, keep my paper diary, keep my savings ticking over like they are. At the union meeting in spring I'd still push for the yearly rise, same as always, because prices for food and fuel keep going up whether AI works or not. Nothing else really changes for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a weight I didn't know I was carrying just lifted. I'd feel a bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the manager might cut a body. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Derek on the arable side, he's sixty-one and does a lot of the field records. If a program does his records, they might decide he's only half a job. I'd fight for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the job you'd let the software have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk recording, maybe, if somebody else types it in. But the calving diary stays on paper. My dad kept one, I keep one, and I've never lost a calf because a phone battery died.

say: I'd tell the canteen that the **AI hype** came to a smarter spreadsheet and nothing more.
I'd post on the union chat that **no computer** calves a heifer at three in the morning.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, because my job, pay and home life all carry on as before.
My one real worry is the manager using saved time to **cut staff** from the yard.
do: Keep milking and keeping the **paper calving diary** exactly as I do now.
Push for the **yearly pay rise** at the spring union meeting, same as every year.
feel: I feel **relieved** and a little **smug** about being right.
S0.quote: A computer that can't calve a heifer at three in the morning was never going to take my job.
fieldNote: His **resistance** to tech is rooted in family habit, like the paper calving diary his father kept.
He thinks first of **protecting colleagues**, naming Derek, before thinking of himself.
Job, savings and a partner in nursing give him **real security** in this picture.

steps.text: Keep the morning milking and paper calving diary at Brookfield
Push for the yearly pay rise through the farm union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the desk jobs get it first, and we get it later. I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office folk who should be worried this time, not us. Down at the co-op they already use software for feed orders and booking the vet, and that'll just take the lot. The office at the co-op will get thinner, and the yard at Brookfield will keep needing a man in wellies for a good while yet. I'd say that, and then I'd say the union needs to be at the table early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried about this year or next. But the co-op already looked at robot milkers in 2024 and said too dear, and in this picture they get cheaper every year. I'd give it five or six years before someone at a board meeting asks why they pay two herdsmen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working, because there's plenty of work for a good stockman. At the union I'd push for a written agreement that nobody gets laid off for a robot without retraining and a year's notice. I won't learn the software myself unless they make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, like hearing thunder on a hot day. Not raining yet, but you start bringing the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the software unless they make you. What if they do make you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn the bit they make me learn and nothing more. Piotr can be the clever one with the tablet. I'd rather spend the time with the cows than with a screen telling me what the cows are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if jobs went at Brookfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the co-op members, they're farmers like me. I'd blame the machine makers and the big supermarkets squeezing the milk price, because that's what makes a board reach for a robot.

say: I'd say the **office jobs** at the co-op will thin out long before the yard does.
I'd tell the union to get a **seat at the table** early, before any machines arrive.
think: Privately I think **robot milkers** get cheap enough within five or six years to threaten a herdsman's post.
My own job feels **safe for now**, but the clock has started ticking.
do: Push the union for a **written agreement**: retraining and a year's notice before any robot job cuts.
Keep working as normal and learn only the **software they require**.
feel: I feel **unsettled**, like thunder on a hot day before the rain starts.
S1.quote: The office at the co-op will get thinner, and the yard at Brookfield will keep needing a man in wellies for a good while yet.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that **desk work** goes first and hands-on work later.
His answer to change is **collective protection**, not learning new tools himself.
He blames **machine makers** and supermarkets rather than the farmers on the co-op board.

steps.text: Keep running the dairy yard at Brookfield as normal
Ask the union for a no-layoff deal without retraining and notice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's next harvest and the one after. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government with a spine. If the machines can do the work, the people who own them should pay for it. I'd be loud about it, probably louder than Ama would like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I'm out of a job around 2031, maybe 2032. The thinking bits like feed planning go in 2028, and then the robots come for the milking and the tractor. Two years isn't enough time for a union to win anything, and five years isn't enough for a herdsman to become something else. I'd be thirty-two with no plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on anything big; we were looking at a new car, and that's off. I'd get the union to push our MP for a law on notice and redundancy pay for farmworkers replaced by machines. And I'd sit down with Ama and work out whether her wage covers the house if mine goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like when the vet tells you it's TB and the whole herd has to be tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ama's wage might have to cover the house. Would her job be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nursing's hands-on too, so maybe she gets the same three years I do. The charting and rotas will go to the AI first, and she hates the charting anyway. But if both of us are in the robot queue at once, that's a bad night at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd retrain for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People keep saying fix the robots, but I'm not a mechanic and I'm not going to become one at thirty. I'd rather fight to keep people on the farms. If that fails, I don't know, and I don't like not knowing.

say: I'd say loudly that **robot owners** should pay for the workers their machines replace.
I'd tell people this is why we need **strong unions** and a government with a spine.
think: Privately I expect to **lose my job** around 2031, when robots take the milking and tractor work.
I don't believe a union can win much in **two years**, and I've got no plan B.
do: Cancel the **new car** and stop all big spending straight away.
Get the union to lobby our **MP** for notice and redundancy rules for replaced farmworkers.
Work out with Ama whether **her wage** alone covers the house.
feel: I feel **sick**, like hearing the herd has TB.
I'm **scared** of not knowing what comes after.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time for a union to win anything, and five years isn't enough for a herdsman to become something else.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** by about 2031 and says so plainly.
He rejects **retraining** as a mechanic, which leaves him with no fallback.
The **household** is exposed too, since Ama's nursing is hands-on and in the same robot queue.
His strong savings buy time, but he sees **no plan** to spend that time on.

steps.text: Cancel the new car and put that money into savings
Get the union to lobby the local MP on robot redundancy rules
Organise farm staff across the co-op to demand notice and payouts
Plan with Ama to live on her nursing wage if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking machines, eight for the robots. All right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, just with more time to organise. I'd say on the union chat that we've got five years to get rules in place, so let's not waste them. I'd want every farmworker in the county signed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still ends with a robot in my parlour, just in 2034 instead of 2031. Five years is long enough for the union to fight and for me to buy my grandad's twelve acres, and I want both. Owning land means at least something is mine when the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd offer my two cousins a fair price for their share of grandad's land; I've got the savings to do it. I'd run for the union's regional committee, which I've avoided for years. And I'd keep putting a third of my wage away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less sick than the fast one. More like preparing for a hard winter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with twelve acres?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep a few suckler cows and some hens, sell beef boxes to people in town. It wouldn't pay a wage, but it's something no robot owner can take off me. My dad would like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like new technology, but would you use a robot on your own twelve acres?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, on twelve acres it's not worth it. That's the funny thing: the small places might be the last ones with people on them.

say: I'd tell the union chat we have **five years** to get rules in place and shouldn't waste them.
I'd urge every **farmworker** in the county to sign up.
think: Privately it still ends with a **robot in my parlour**, just three years later.
Owning **grandad's land** would mean something is mine when the job goes.
do: Offer my cousins a fair price for their share of **grandad's twelve acres**.
Stand for the union's **regional committee**, which I've avoided for years.
Keep saving **a third** of my wage every month.
feel: I feel **worried** but steadier, like preparing for a hard winter.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for the union to fight and for me to buy my grandad's twelve acres, and I want both.
fieldNote: Extra time turns his fear into **two plans**: union organising and owning land.
He still expects to **lose his job** around 2034, just later than in the fast picture.
He notices that **small farms** might keep people on them longest.

steps.text: Buy out his cousins' shares of grandad's twelve acres
Stand for the union's regional committee this year
Save a third of his monthly wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and then three more. I'd be near forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this properly, so let's use it. With ten years I can fight for a rule that says a farm robot pays a tax like a worker pays a tax. I'd say that at the union and to anyone who'd listen down the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like forever to me, and that's the danger. I'd probably carry on as I am for five or six of them and only get serious later. Ama would tell me that's exactly what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd keep working at Brookfield and keep saving as normal. I'd join the union campaign for a robot tax and vote for whoever backs it. Past that, I'd wait and see what the machines actually look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little itch at the back of my mind. It's on my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only get serious later. What would getting serious look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe buying the twelve acres after all, or moving to a smaller farm where they can't afford robots. I'd decide around 2032, when I can see what the machines do on other farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young lad starting at Brookfield in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young lad starting at Brookfield to learn the cows properly anyway, because knowing animals never goes to waste. And I'd tell him to join the union on his first day.

say: I'd say we have **time** to do it **properly** and should use it.
I'd argue at the union and the pub for a **robot tax** like a worker's tax.
think: Privately I know I'd **put it off** for five or six years because ten feels like forever.
My job and income feel **safe for now**, though it's on my mind.
do: Keep working at **Brookfield** and saving as normal for the first few years.
Back the union's **robot tax** campaign and vote for whoever supports it.
Decide around **2032** whether to buy land or move to a smaller farm.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, with a small itch at the back of my mind.
S4.quote: With ten years I can fight for a rule that says a farm robot pays a tax like a worker pays a tax.
fieldNote: He admits he would **procrastinate**, which is honest self-knowledge for a resistant man.
His focus stays on **fair shares** of robot earnings, not on adapting himself.
He sets a **decision point** of 2032 rather than acting now.

steps.text: Keep milking and saving at Brookfield for the next few years
Vote for candidates who back a tax on farm robots
Watch robots on other farms before deciding about land in 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no question. If I lost the job at Brookfield in 2031, what would help is proper notice, redundancy pay and maybe a share of what the robots earn. I don't want a robot to be clever, I want the man who owns the robot to share what it earns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Nobody ever does. A robot might milk them fine, but someone has to care whether they're happy, and I'm not sure a co-op board counts that.

headlineQuote: I don't want a robot to be clever, I want the man who owns the robot to share what it earns.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old herdsman** on a co-op dairy farm, living with Ama, a hospital nurse.
He has **over a year saved** and a share of his grandad's twelve acres.
He's a **union rep** who avoids new tech and keeps his calving diary on paper.
He moves from **calm** about hype to **alarmed** in the two-year picture, expecting robots to take his job.
With more time he plans to **organise** and buy land rather than retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because robots could take his job by 2031 with no plan B.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **notice and redundancy pay** for replaced farmworkers.
He wants robot owners to **share the earnings** with the people they replace.
